Years 11–13 Technology – Digital

Learning expectations
Through Technology, students are taught that effective and ethical design respects the unique
relationship between people and their physical environment, and embraces the significance of
culture and world views in technological practice and innovation.

The learning area supports students to be innovative, reflective, and critical in designing new
models, products, software, systems, and tools to benefit people while taking account of their
impact on cultural, ethical, environmental, and economic conditions.


Key features of the refreshed learning area
•   Clear progression from Years 9–10 through to advanced specialist technology pathways.
•   Explicit teaching of disciplinary writing and communication so students can explain processes,
    interpret evidence, and justify design and technical decisions.
•   Greater visibility of responsible practice, including cultural, ethical, environmental, social,
    privacy, safety and sustainability considerations.
•   Purpose-built pathways that support students with different interests, strengths, and future
    aspirations.
•   Strong connections between theory and authentic real-world contexts, including industry,
    science, engineering, creative technologies, digital systems and community needs.
•   Strong connections between disciplinary knowledge and practical application through
    programming, designing, constructing, testing, troubleshooting and refinement.


Subjects
Subjects within the Technology – Digital learning area are:

•   Year 11 Digital Technologies
•   Years 12–13 Computer Science
•   Years 12–13 Digital Media
•   Years 12–13 Electronics and Mechatronics.

Learning and pathways

Year 11 Digital Technologies
Students are taught how to investigate needs and opportunities, design purposeful outcomes, and
develop, test, refine, and evaluate their work. Depending on the strand selected, students apply
knowledge and practices from computational thinking and programming, digital media, or
electronics and mechatronic systems to create outcomes for specific users, purposes, and
contexts.

Strands

Year 11 Digital Technologies is organised into three strands:

•   Electronics and Mechatronics
•   Digital Technologies
•   Disciplinary Writing.
Year 11 Digital Technologies is designed with a constrained choice to support teaching and
learning. Schools should choose one of two subject strands, either Electronics and Mechatronics
or Digital Technologies, to be taught alongside disciplinary writing.

Programme design

Schools select either the Digital Technologies strand or the Electronics and Mechatronics strand.
While all knowledge and practices within the selected strand are compulsory, schools determine
how they are organised across the year. Learning may draw together content from different
elements where this supports the coherent development of disciplinary knowledge and practical
capability. Programmes should provide explicit teaching of foundational knowledge and technical
skills, followed by opportunities to apply this learning through the design, development, testing,
refinement and evaluation of digital or electronic outcomes.

Pathways

Year 11 Digital Technologies provides foundations for Years 12–13 Computer Science, Years 12–
13 Digital Media, and Year 12–13 Electronics and Mechatronics. This subject supports learning
across science, mathematics and statistics, commerce, health, social sciences, and many other
learning areas.

Years 12–13 Computer Science
Students are taught to apply computational thinking, manage and analyse data, design and
develop software, and evaluate algorithms, programs and computational systems. They are taught
to formulate problems, create and refine algorithms and programs, represent and manage data,
and evaluate digital systems in terms of efficiency, reliability, security, and usability. Students also
examine the broader implications of digital systems and emerging technologies, including privacy,
cybersecurity, bias, data sovereignty, and the responsible use.

Strands

Years 12–13 Computer Science is organised into five strands:

•   Computational Thinking
•   Data, Information, and Digital Systems
•   Software Design and Development
•   Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

Programmes should develop connected knowledge and practice across computational thinking,
data and digital systems, software design and development, and artificial intelligence and emerging
technologies. Content may be taught through separate areas of study or integrated through
suitable computational problems and software-development contexts. Programmes should provide
regular opportunities to interpret, design, implement, test, debug, analyse and evaluate algorithms,
programs, data and computational systems.

Pathways

Years 12–13 Computer Science leads to pathways in computer science and related disciplines
such as software engineering, data science, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, information
systems, digital technologies and technology innovation.

Years 12–13 Digital Media
Students are taught how digital media can be used to communicate information, experiences, and
ideas through interactive, information, and time-based media. They are taught how design
principles, conventions, user experience, technical production processes, and responsible
practices influence the development of digital media outcomes.

Strands

Years 12–13 Digital Media is organised into five strands:

•   Project Management
•   Digital Media Foundations
•   Define and Design

•   Develop, Release, and Evaluate
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

Programmes should integrate learning from across the strands and apply it through interactive,
information, or time-based media contexts. This may involve one or more appropriately scoped
projects. Projects should provide sufficient opportunities for students to develop technical skills,
make informed design and production decisions, gather evidence through testing and feedback,
refine their work, and evaluate the final digital media outcome.

Pathways

Years 12–13 Digital Media leads to pathways in screen industries, web and app development,
creative technologies, interactive media, animation, and game development.

Years 12–13 Electronics and Mechatronics
Students are taught to apply engineering principles to investigate problems and opportunities, and
to design, test, and refine integrated systems. They are taught to use iterative processes to
analyse system behaviour, evaluate performance, and develop innovative solutions that respond
effectively to identified needs and system requirements.

Strands

Years 12–13 Electronics and Mechatronics is organised into five strands:

•   Sensing and Measurement
•   Actuation and Response
•   Controlling System Behaviour
•   System Integration
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

Programmes should connect learning across all strands of the curriculum. Students should be
explicitly taught relevant electronic, mechanical, programming, communication and systems
knowledge before and during its practical application. Learning should include opportunities to
construct and test circuits, mechanisms, control methods, and subsystems before these are
integrated into complete systems.

Pathways

Years 12–13 Electronics and Mechatronics leads to pathways in engineering, communication
systems, robotics, electronics, industrial and product design, trades, and applied technologies.

How to design a programme
•   The knowledge and practice statements within each element are related, but teachers may
    select complementary statements from across strands and elements to support coherence and
    depth within a project. Disciplinary writing is most effectively taught when integrated across the
    teaching programme.
•   Technology subjects are inherently project-based, with projects providing contexts for students
    to apply, connect, and demonstrate prescribed knowledge and practices. Projects should be
    appropriately scoped to support explicit teaching, technical and practical skill development,
    informed decision-making, testing, refining and evaluation.


Connections to other learning areas
Technology connects strongly with:

•   Science through measurement, electronics, energy, forces, systems, experimentation, and
    data analysis.
•   Mathematics and Statistics through measurement, scale, geometry, calculation, modelling,
    data interpretation, tolerances, and quantitative evaluation.
•   English through disciplinary writing, technical communication, explanation, evaluation, and
    evidence-based justification.
•   Social Sciences through the cultural, social, ethical, economic, and societal implications of
    technological development.
•   The Arts through visual communication, interaction, animation, screen production, sound,
    composition, and creative technologies.
•   Commerce through digital enterprise, project management, information systems, innovation,
    and the development of digital products and services.
•   The digital-focused Technology subjects also connect with Food Processing Technology,
    Resistant Materials Technology, Textiles Technology, and Spatial and Product Design, through
    shared knowledge and practices relating to design, technical development, project
    management, testing, refinement, responsible practice, and evaluation. See Technology
    Information Sheet for further information about these subjects.
